title: Restaurant catering marketing that wins local office orders

question: How do I market catering to local offices as a restaurant owner?

intro:
Restaurant catering marketing to local offices starts with one rule: make it easy for an office manager to place a large order on a busy day. The fastest wins usually come from a clear catering menu, a direct phone line, and a simple follow-up process.

For independent restaurants, the goal is not fancy marketing. It is being the easy choice when an office needs lunch for 10, 25, or 50 people. That means your menu, hours, phone script, and follow-up all need to work together.

sections.h2: Which offices should you target first?
sections.body:
Start close to home. Nearby offices are easier to reach, easier to deliver to, and more likely to order again if the first order goes well. Think about law offices, real estate offices, medical offices, construction offices, coworking spaces, schools, and local shops with staff lunch needs.

Make a short list and work in a tight circle around your restaurant. A simple approach is better than blasting everyone:

1. List 25 offices within a short drive.
2. Write down the office name, address, main phone, and any public email.
3. Note whether they seem to have daily staff lunch, meetings, or client visits.
4. Put the most promising 10 offices at the top.

Here is a practical filter:

| Office type | Why it can work | What to offer |
|---|---|---|
| Law or accounting office | Regular staff lunches and meetings | Sandwich platters, hot trays, salads |
| Medical office | Fast, tidy lunch orders | Individually packed meals |
| Construction office | Larger orders and early timing | Hearty trays, breakfast catering |
| Coworking space | Repeat lunch and event orders | Mix-and-match platters |

Use wording that sounds local and simple: “We’re nearby and can handle lunch for your team on short notice.”

sections.h2: What should your catering offer look like?
sections.body:
Office buyers want clarity. They do not want to decode a full menu at 11:20 a.m. Build a catering offer that is easy to quote and easy to repeat. Keep it narrow at first: a few platters, a few trays, and a few add-ons.

A good menu for office catering usually includes:

- Sandwich or wrap platters
- Hot trays or pasta trays
- Salad trays
- Breakfast trays for early meetings
- Drinks and simple sides
- Disposable plates, napkins, and utensils

Use names that make ordering simple. Instead of a long dish description, use practical labels like “small tray,” “serves 8–10,” or “feeds 15.” Then train staff to quote from the same structure every time.

A useful phone line for this is: “I can help with catering. How many people are you feeding, and what time do you need it ready?”

Also, be clear about what your restaurant can handle. If you need advance notice for large orders, say so. If certain items are sold out, the phone host should not offer them. ROAL reads the live menu and does not offer items marked sold out, which helps keep office quotes realistic. The cleaner your offer, the easier it is to turn inquiries into actual tickets.

sections.h2: How do you market catering without sounding pushy?
sections.body:
You do not need a big campaign. You need a steady pattern. Local office catering marketing works best when your message is useful, short, and easy to act on.

Try these three channels first:

1. Drop off a small printed sheet with your catering menu at nearby offices.
2. Send a short email or message to office managers with a direct phone number.
3. Ask current takeout customers who work nearby whether their office orders lunch.

Keep the message focused on convenience. Example: “Need lunch for the team? Call us with the headcount and time, and we’ll help you choose a tray order that fits.”

A simple follow-up script helps too: “I wanted to check whether your office has lunch orders coming up this week. We can handle small teams or larger group meals.”

If your restaurant already gets a lot of phone traffic, keep your marketing tied to the phone. ROAL can answer routine questions, take pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, and hand catering requests to staff with a summary. That means your team spends less time repeating the same details and more time closing real catering orders.

For a deeper look at phone-first demand, see [catering inquiries](/use-cases/catering) and [phone orders vs delivery apps](/compare/delivery-apps).

sections.h2: What should you say when an office calls?
sections.body:
The first call often decides the order. Office buyers want speed, clarity, and a real person or a reliable phone host that can get details right. Your script should ask the few questions that matter most, in the same order every time.

Use a short flow like this:

- “How many people are you feeding?”
- “What day and time do you need it?”
- “Do you want individual lunches or platters?”
- “Any allergies or special requests?”
- “What name and phone number should we put on the order?”

Then repeat it back: “So I have a lunch catering order for 18 people, Thursday at 12:30, with mixed sandwich platters, two salads, and no mushrooms. Is that right?”

That repeat-back matters. It catches mistakes before food is made. It also builds trust with office managers who place group orders often.

ROAL can take catering requests on the phone, collect the caller’s name and phone, and hand the request to staff with a summary. It also takes allergy-sensitive questions and manager requests to staff when needed. It does not take card numbers over the phone, so payment still happens the way your restaurant already handles it.

If you want a few ready-made lines, [phone greeting templates](/tools/phone-greeting-templates) can help you tighten the first minute of the call.

sections.h2: How should you price office catering?
sections.body:
Pricing should be easy to quote and easy to defend. Office buyers usually want a total they can understand quickly. They do not want a long back-and-forth over every topping.

A simple way to think about it is by order size. For example, say your average office order is $28 per person. A 12-person lunch would be about $336 before any extras. A 20-person order would be about $560. Those are only example numbers, so plug in your own menu prices and local costs.

Use a basic pricing structure like this:

| Order type | How to price it |
|---|---|
| Small team lunch | Per person or per platter |
| Medium office order | Set bundles with add-ons |
| Large meeting or event | Custom quote with prep time |

If delivery apps take a commission, that can cut into a large order fast. If you handle office catering by phone, you keep more control over the order details and the relationship. You also avoid the fixed monthly fee problem that many AI phone tools and human answering services have, because ROAL charges per completed phone order instead of a monthly fee.

sections.h2: How do you keep office catering from falling through the cracks?
sections.body:
Office catering breaks down when the phone rings, the kitchen is busy, and nobody writes the details clearly. The fix is a simple system that catches the order, confirms it, and gets it to the kitchen fast.

Use a short checklist every time:

1. Confirm headcount.
2. Confirm date and ready time.
3. Confirm menu items and quantities.
4. Ask about allergies and special notes.
5. Confirm contact name and phone.
6. Send the order to the kitchen.

A clean example: “We have the order for 14 lunches, Thursday at 11:45, with 7 turkey wraps, 4 chicken salads, and 3 veggie wraps. I’ll send it through now.”

This is where ROAL fits naturally. It sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen, and the dashboard keeps call history with transcripts and recordings. If a question comes in that the host cannot answer, it lands in an inbox. The owner answers once, and the host knows it from then on. That keeps office inquiries from bouncing around between shifts.

If you want to improve your phone flow, review [how it works](/how-it-works) and [rush-hour phone orders](/use-cases/rush-hour). Even a small restaurant can look more organized when the same details are captured every time.

sections.h2: How do you set up your phone so office orders are easier to catch?
sections.body:
A lot of catering sales are lost because the phone setup is clumsy. Office managers call during lunch, then get voicemail, a busy signal, or a rushed answer. Make the phone simple to reach and simple to hand off.

A practical setup looks like this:

- Keep your restaurant’s main number.
- Forward calls when busy or unanswered.
- Use a separate path for office catering inquiries when you need it.
- Test the forwarding with a real call before lunch rush.

On many carriers and landlines, forwarding codes vary. Some common examples are *72 to forward all calls and *73 to turn it off, while some mobile carriers use codes like **21*number# for all calls or **61*number# for unanswered calls. Verizon Wireless uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually set this in the web portal. Always confirm with your carrier and test it with a call.

ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically once you claim the host, and you can forward your existing number to it. Forwarding can be turned off any time, so you stay in control. If you want to try it, [build a free test host](/try) from your website, Google Maps link, or restaurant name and city.

Before you go live, check this:

- Can the host answer hours and address correctly?
- Does it read the live menu?
- Does it handle catering questions?
- Does the kitchen see the ticket clearly?

takeaways: Start with nearby offices that can reorder often.
Keep catering menus simple, priced clearly, and easy to quote.
Use a phone script that confirms headcount, timing, and special requests.
Make sure kitchen tickets are clean and fast to read.
Phone setup matters as much as promotion when office orders come in.

faq.q: How do I get local offices to order catering from my restaurant?
faq.a: Start with offices within a short drive and contact the people who handle lunch: office managers, admins, and receptionists. Offer a simple menu, a clear phone number, and fast quoting. A short message like “We can handle lunch for your team and help you pick the right tray order” is usually more useful than a long pitch.

faq.q: What should I include in a restaurant catering menu for offices?
faq.a: Keep it narrow and easy to quote. Sandwich platters, salad trays, hot trays, breakfast trays, and drinks are common starting points. Add clear serving sizes, simple labels, and notes for utensils or napkins so the office buyer can place the order quickly.

faq.q: Should I use delivery apps for office catering orders?
faq.a: You can, but delivery apps commonly charge restaurants roughly 15-30% commission per order, which can hurt margin on larger catering jobs. Many owners prefer to get office catering orders by phone so they can keep more control over the details, timing, and customer relationship.
